correspondence.component_scope: Chosen eastern opening and initial tie into the upper north-trending branch
correspondence.finding: The easternmost westward opening falls beyond or at the eastern limit of the Zulia hydrographic figure. The Falcón chapter names the Matícora tributaries Riecito and Jordán, but that prose does not identify this chosen feeder or establish its initial connection. The opening and its first join therefore remain unresolved; no local feeder name is assigned.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper north-trending approach and its westward receiving junction
correspondence.finding: The northeastern portion of Figure13 depicts a southern approach turning north into the east–west inflow upstream of Embalse Matícora. The visible branch, its northward course and junction correspond at ordinary regional scale to this selected portion. This establishes the visible connection without assigning the lower Matícora label to every upper tributary.

correspondence.component_scope: Westward receiving corridor and reservoir approach
correspondence.finding: Figure13 carries the joined eastern drainage west across the upland-to-reservoir approach into the Matícora impoundment. The selected westward corridor agrees with that continuous depicted inflow. Regional tributary prose is corroboration only; it does not establish exact Riecito or Jordán name boundaries on the selected route.

correspondence.component_scope: Embalse Matícora passage and northward outlet
correspondence.finding: Figure13 depicts Embalse Matícora between its eastern inflow and the northward Río Matícora outlet. The Falcón chapter independently describes the river as impounded near Mene de Mauroa. Together these support the selected managed-water passage at regional scale; the impoundment crossing is not described as an uninterrupted natural-river reach.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower northwestward and northward Río Matícora
correspondence.finding: The map explicitly labels Río Matícora along the connected outlet and lower course toward the gulf. It places the separate Cocuiza and Palmar drainages farther west, toward Los Olivitos, so those river names and the wetland are not assigned to this selected course.

correspondence.component_scope: Final mouth-facing reach and actual stored endpoint
correspondence.finding: Figure13 connects the lower Matícora to the southern shore of Golfo de Venezuela, and the Falcón chapter explicitly names that receiver. The actual stored endpoint corresponds to gulf water immediately off this outlet at ordinary map scale. It is not replaced by the separate model source endpoint, nor interpreted as a named river continuing through the sea.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen Sierra Agua de Mayo opening and Camargo upper corridor
correspondence.finding: The selected opening and southward course match a mapped stream on the Sierra Agua de Mayo flank and its continuation into the valley labeled Bentín. Nearby Laguna Verde lies west of the selected route; no crossing of that lake is required.

correspondence.component_scope: Camargo–Jiménez transition and upper Bentín joins
correspondence.finding: The selected southeastward municipal transition is depicted by connected blue watercourse lines on both originals. Jiménez repeats Bentín on the northwestern approach to the eastern plain; lateral joins from the Cerros Emilio/Sierra El Diablo setting are visible. The route is separate from the Laguna El Remolino basin to the west.

correspondence.component_scope: Eastern Sierra El Diablo Bentín corridor
correspondence.finding: The selected successive southeast and south stretches follow the mapped Bentín course along the eastern side of Sierra El Diablo. Tributary junctions and the lower El Hundido-side joining setting are depicted. Distinct short line parts are considered as the same connected selected mainstem, without assigning the Bentín name to every unselected tributary.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower Bentín and Palomas approach
correspondence.finding: The mapped southward lower course turns toward the Palomas receiving plain, taking the selected westward bend and joining corridor. The original depicts a continuous incoming watercourse approaching the northern lake-flat margin, rather than requiring an inferred cross-basin shortcut.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual northern Palomas receiving-flat/inlet ending
correspondence.finding: The final selected parts correspond to the northern inlet/receiving-flat setting adjoining Laguna de Palomas, where northern and western mapped watercourses converge. The selection ends there; it does not cross the whole lake or extend to its southern shore. Laguna de los Patos is shown separately to the east. Mapped lake-margin and flat geometry establishes the terminal setting at ordinary scale, without requiring a precise contemporary wet shoreline or persistent surface discharge.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen western opening and northeastward feeder west of Sierra Descubridora
correspondence.finding: The Mapimí relief map depicts an unnamed watercourse rising west of Sierra Descubridora and turning northeast, then north along the eastern side of Cerro Picacho de Ibarra. The chosen opening and consecutive parts correspond at ordinary municipal-map scale. Nearby Santo Domingo and José León belong to distinct mapped approaches and are not assigned to this feeder.

correspondence.component_scope: Northward foothill corridor and intermediate joins east of Cerro Picacho de Ibarra
correspondence.finding: The original Mapimí map shows the northward watercourse through the foothill passage east of Cerro Picacho de Ibarra, with side joins and the northeastward departure into the plain. It also distinguishes the western Cañada Honda and Acebuches approaches and the nearby Boquilla de Acebuches waterbody. A selected crossing of that named waterbody is not asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: El Barroso reach and transition into the El Tordillo surroundings
correspondence.finding: The northeastward-to-eastward plain reach joins the watercourse directly labeled El Barroso on the Mapimí original and continues into the adjoining Tlahualilo map near El Tordillo. The two municipal views support the boundary transition and immediate eastern stream corridor. The small El Tordillo waterbody lies beside this transition; an exact selected lake crossing or a transfer of its name to the stream is not established.

correspondence.component_scope: Southeastward departure from the El Tordillo corridor toward Laguna Colorada
correspondence.finding: The selected southeastward course departs from the mapped stream that runs farther east toward Las Liebres. The Tlahualilo original covers the intervening plain north and northeast of Sierra Banderas, but does not establish the selected through-going connection to Laguna Colorada. Regional closed-basin prose does not resolve this particular passage.

correspondence.component_scope: Laguna Colorada passage beside Sierra Banderas
correspondence.finding: The selected north–south passage corresponds to the mapped Laguna Colorada immediately east of Sierra Banderas. The municipal hydrography table classifies this named waterbody as intermittent. Descroix separately identifies Laguna Colorada among the small northwestern depressions of the La Laguna region. These establish the lake setting, while neither source establishes both selected approach and departure links.

correspondence.component_scope: Southern plain loop and eastward return below Las Liebres
correspondence.finding: The municipal original covers the plain crossed by the selected loop south and east of Laguna Colorada. It separately shows the Las Liebres waterbody and its north–south stream corridor, but no connected channel follows the selected loop from Colorada to that corridor. The scholarly regional map and discussion do not supply a managed-channel, overflow or other specific through-link for this selection.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual inland terminal south of Las Liebres
correspondence.finding: The actual final tip lies in the mapped plain south of Las Liebres and just beyond the north–south corridor associated with that waterbody. It is not independently established as a named river mouth or lake outlet. The incoming selected plain link and terminal hydraulic identity remain unresolved; the endpoint is not extended to a different named lagoon.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen eastern opening and connection into the Palmadera/upper San Juan setting
correspondence.finding: Detailed map P depicts Jeñuascancha, Sacsa and other neighboring upper feeders, lakes, the Palmadera course and a proposed storage footprint. The selected eastern feeder and every connection into that course cannot be distinguished securely from this map, regional map13.1 and schematic E7. Nearby names and basin membership are not sufficient to identify the selected opening.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper San Juan and the Colcabamba–Tantará joining setting
correspondence.finding: Map13.1 shows the westward upper Río San Juan course, its tributary relationship to the Huichinga lake-drainage system and the joining Colcabamba course, followed by the southwestward Tantará reach near Aurahuá and Chupamarca. Map P, schematic E0/E7 and pp64–65 supply the same joining hierarchy. This supports the ordinary corridor after the unresolved headward approach.

correspondence.component_scope: Tantará southward course and Huachos/Arma confluence
correspondence.finding: The mapped Tantará course bends south past the Tantará/Huamatambo setting and continues toward San Juan de Castrovirreyna. The eastern Arma/Huachos drainage joins near the lower turn. The source prose explicitly distinguishes Tantará from the downstream San Juan name; the junction and selected southward course agree at corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Middle San Juan southward and westward bends
correspondence.finding: Map13.1 continuously depicts the San Juan course below the Huachos joining setting, passing the Capillas side-drainage setting and then turning west toward the lower valley. The successive selected bends and joining tributaries correspond to that course. Prose and E0 distinguish Ayoque and Almacén as lower incoming drainages rather than substitute names for the main course.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower joining corridor and managed partition at Conta
correspondence.finding: The selected lower course enters the Chincha valley and follows the northern arm at the lower partition. Page145 identifies Conta as a hydraulic partition structure and calls Río Chico an earth channel receiving San Juan water. The map and E9 distinguish Chico from the other lower course, Matagente. This managed connection is part of the selected route; no present operating state is inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Northern Río Chico channel and actual Pacific terminal
correspondence.finding: Map13.1 traces the labeled Río Chico west through the lower valley to the Pacific shoreline at Tambo de Mora, separately north of the Matagente outlet. E9 also depicts the Chico branch reaching the ocean. This identifies the actual selected coastward corridor independently of the supplied sea flag, without claiming an exact mouth vertex or current opening.
